title: Pharmacy stock and refills
like: a pharmacy chain's stock and refill system
brief: A pharmacy chain with 4,000 stores tracks how many boxes of each medicine every store has, takes refill requests, and shows patients which nearby store has their medicine today. If the system says a store has a box that is gone, a patient makes a wasted trip.

clarify.q: How wrong may a stock count be?
clarify.a: For browsing, a few seconds late is fine. For handing out a controlled medicine, the count must be exact at the moment of sale.
Yes. Head office runs big stock reports during the night and again in the morning. They are heavy.

clarify.q: Is one medicine ever far more popular than others?
clarify.a: Yes. A flu season or a shortage can make one product ID hold a third of all lookups.

clarify.q: Are patients told when a refill is ready?
clarify.a: Yes, by push or text. It can arrive a minute late, but not twice.

notes: Each store sends a stock event every time a box is scanned in or out.
A "write" here is a dispense or a refill order.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Stock events from scanners at peak

hints: Which requests must be exact, and which can be a little behind? Send the first to the main copy and the second to a copy.
Search on "which store has it" is a different job from keeping the count. A search index fed from the database by change data capture is the usual split.
Out-of-order events must not resurrect sold stock; physical inventory still needs reconciliation. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: The same stock number is used for two things: an exact count at the till and a roughly-right count for browsing. The design splits them. The database owns the exact count; a search index and a warehouse are copies that can be a little behind and keep their load off it.

designs.name: One truth, two copies
designs.why: A sharded SQL database keeps the exact count with synchronous copies and answers the short stock reports a manager asks for. Change data capture feeds a search index for "which store has it" and a data warehouse for the heavy analysis, which never sits behind a user click. Notices and bulk stock events ride queues.

tradeoffs: The search index can be a few seconds behind. That is fine for "who has it nearby", and the till still checks the exact count before dispensing.
Reports in a warehouse cost another $1,800 a month and take the heavy job off the live database; running them on the main database is free until a morning where it is not.
A tiny cache with coalescing makes the very popular product cost one database read per few seconds instead of thousands.
Sharding by store spreads writes, but one store's big night can still fall on one shard.
editorial.realWorld: A large pharmacy chain handles on the order of hundreds of stock events a second at peak (approx.), and replica lag in a healthy managed database is usually well under a second, but can reach tens of seconds during heavy writes or maintenance.

correctness.prompt: Pharmacy stock and refills: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Distinguish stale stock discovery from authoritative reservation. Search freshness is not a stock ownership guarantee. The reservation transaction prevents overselling. Out-of-order events must not resurrect sold stock; physical inventory still needs reconciliation.

fields.label: Step 1. Search says one box remains, but a store just sold it. May refill promise it?
options: Recheck authoritative store stock when reserving
fields.explanation: Search freshness is not a stock ownership guarantee.

fields.label: Step 2. Two refills claim that last box. What commits?
options: Two inserts after separate availability reads
One atomic conditional reservation with a unique refill id

fields.label: Step 3. A delayed sale update arrives after a newer count. Apply it blindly?
options: Use source versions and reconcile discrepancies against store inventory
fields.explanation: Out-of-order events must not resurrect sold stock; physical inventory still needs reconciliation.

correctness.responsibility: Distinguish stale stock discovery from authoritative reservation.
